name: Dariusz Nwosu-Caballero
subcategory: Shelf zine publisher and spoken-word artist
creator: Dariusz Nwosu-Caballero
description: Operating out of a repurposed water reclamation substation in Shelf District 7, Nwosu-Caballero has published forty-three issues of 'Floodmark Quarterly' — a physically printed zine distributed by hand in Tier 1 and 2 circuits — while simultaneously running a pirate neural feed channel called Open Ear where he delivers spoken-word pieces directly into the BCI stream, raw and uncompressed, without the smoothing filters that corporate neural content requires by law. His voice work is characterized by extreme tonal range, sudden silence used as punctuation, and a habit of embedding the names of real Compact enforcement officers into his verses. He has been cited for unlicensed neural broadcast seven times; each citation has become source material.
medium: physical zine, pirate neural feed (unfiltered spoken word)
cultural_impact: Floodmark Quarterly is one of the longest-running continuously published independent zines in GLMZ and has become an informal archive of Shelf life — births, deaths, disputes, small dignities — that no corponation media outlet would record.
controversy: His practice of naming Compact enforcement officers in his verse has resulted in two harassment complaints from officers' unions and one informal threat of infrastructure action against his district's power allocation. His supporters argue this is precisely the point. The unfiltered neural broadcasts technically violate BCI content safety standards, which he argues were written to protect corporations, not listeners.
story_hooks: Issue 44 of Floodmark Quarterly contains information — embedded in a poem, possibly inadvertently — that a corponation would pay significantly to suppress.
Nwosu-Caballero goes silent for six weeks; the Shelf community must determine whether he has been detained, gone dark voluntarily, or something else entirely.
A Tier 4 literary institution offers to archive all 43 issues of Floodmark Quarterly, and the terms of the offer reveal exactly what they think the zine is for.
